newsitem.title: USA: IBM results seen on track when it reports Monday.
newsitem.headline: IBM results seen on track when it reports Monday.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp. is expected to post solid, on-track earnings when it reports second quarter results on Monday, though some analysts foresee an upside surprise.
The average estimate is $1.42 a share, according to First Call, versus $1.26 a year ago, after adjusting for a 2-for-1 stock split. Analysts' estimates ranged from from $1.36 to $1.50 a share.
This quarter will also be the first without IBM's chief financial officer, G. Richard Thoman, who left IBM last month to become the number two executive at Xerox Corp.

The results are due out after the market closes on Monday. In a change this quarter, IBM will not host its usual face-to-face meeting with analysts, but instead will conduct its quarterly analysts' meeting in a conference call at 4:30 p.m. EDT (2030 GMT).

Lawrence Ricciardi, IBM's senior vice president and chief counsel, will preside over the conference call as interim chief financial officer, since IBM has not yet named a CFO. The computer giant will also use the Internet for the first time with Wall Street, putting financial slides on its Web site for discussion when the call begins.
Analysts said they expect IBM's second quarter to mirror its first quarter in some ways, but with smaller currency-related losses.

In the 1997 first quarter, IBM reported earnings of about $1.2 billion, or $2.37 a share before the stock split, on sales of $17.3 billion. In the second quarter a year ago, IBM earned $1.3 billion, or $2.51 a share before the split, on sales of $18.2 billion.

But AS/400 minicomputers sales are expected to improve slightly from the first quarter. Mainframes will also show an improvement over the first quarter, due to sales of a new mainframe model, called the G4, which IBM began shipping in June. But mainframe revenues will still be down versus last year, analysts said.

"It will be a good quarter," said Milunovich, adding that the buzz on Wall Street has been fairly quiet, unlike last quarter, when there were rumours -- which proved to be false -- that IBM would come in below expectations.
Analysts said that IBM will again see its revenues and earnings negatively hit by the stronger dollar, but the impact will be less than in the first quarter.

On a pre-split basis, IBM's first-quarter earnings reflected a negative impact from currency fluctations of 19 cents a share, with the dollar's strength against the Japanese yen viewed as the biggest factor.
"It was definitely less of a hit than last quarter," said Bill Milton, a Brown Brothers Harriman analyst.

Gary Helmig of SoundView Financial Group said this week that IBM's shares did not participate in the broader technology stock rally because of fears about the negative impact of the dollar's strength against the German mark, which sparked investor jitters about the third quarter.
Helmig said both quarters are "fine." He is looking for $1.42 a share Monday.

Helmig made bullish comments about IBM on Thursday about the possibility for expansion of IBM's current price/earnings ratio. Helmig's comments, combined with Mandresh's move to raise his price target on Friday, helped fuel interest in IBM's shares. IBM has risen 6.5 percent in the past two days, from Wednesday's close of 97-5/8.
